interviews.person: Elon Musk (CEO of SpaceX and Tesla)
interviews.venue: The Sean Hannity Show (radio), guest-hosted by Texas Governor Greg Abbott
interviews.summary:
Elon Musk joined guest host Texas Governor Greg Abbott on the Sean Hannity Show for a call-in segment focused almost entirely on SpaceX — its current operations, Starlink, moon and Mars ambitions, space-based data centers, and employee stock ownership — with a closing exchange about Texas. The most newsworthy items were Musk's stated timelines: potentially landing astronauts on the moon within two to three years, sending the first people to Mars in about five years, and launching the company's "first AI satellites" next year, scaling to "large scale" data centers in space within about two years.

## SpaceX's Current Operations
1. **Starlink as core business:** Musk described SpaceX's satellite launches as primarily serving the Starlink internet system, which he said provides "global high-bandwidth internet connectivity" reaching anywhere from Texas to the poles or the middle of the ocean, calling it "the only such system that exists in the world."
2. **NASA astronaut and cargo transport:** Musk said SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft is the only NASA-qualified vehicle for transporting astronauts to and from the International Space Station besides Russia's Soyuz, and that SpaceX also resupplies the station with cargo and scientific experiments, carrying both US and international astronauts.
3. **Launch market share:** Musk stated SpaceX delivers "about 85% of all the payloads to orbit of Earth," with China accounting for roughly 8% of the remainder and the rest of the world (including the rest of the US) making up about 7% — meaning SpaceX transports "almost 10 times as many satellites to orbit as the rest of the world combined."

## Moon and Mars Ambitions
1. **Moon base within 5 years, city within 10:** Musk said he hopes SpaceX has landed its first people on the moon "in less than five years," with a possibility of putting the first astronauts there in two to three years "if things go well," expanding to "thousands of people on the moon" within roughly 10 years.
2. **Vision of a lunar metropolis:** He described wanting a "full-blown self-sustaining city on the moon — like an actual metropolis," open eventually to any member of the public who wants to go, whether for a vacation or a permanent move, framing the effort as making "science fiction not fiction."
3. **Starship's scale:** Musk said the Starship system is "designed to carry ultimately tens of thousands of tons to the moon."
4. **Mars timeline:** Musk explained Mars launch windows occur only once every 26 months and the trip takes about six months (versus a few days to the moon), but said "if things go well, we can probably send the first people to Mars in about five years," with the cadence increasing every two years thereafter, and hopefully "thousands of people" sent to Mars within a "10-or-12-year timeframe."
5. **Overarching mission:** Musk framed SpaceX's purpose as expanding "life and consciousness as we know it beyond Earth... to the rest of the solar system, and eventually to other star systems."

## Space-Based Data Centers
1. **Compute expansion in space:** Musk said the way to expand computing capacity without consuming Earth's land is to build data centers in space, noting Earth receives "about half a billionth of the sun's energy."
2. **Timeline:** He said SpaceX will "probably be launching our first AI satellites next year," scaling to large-scale deployment "in about two years."

## Employee Stock Ownership
1. **Broad-based equity philosophy:** Musk said his philosophy "from day one" has been that everyone at the company should receive stock, citing a welder who started around 2015 at about $28/hour as one of "several thousand people" on the production line whose stock, if they joined early, is "probably worth over a million dollars at this point."

## Texas Ties
1. **Texas flag emoji commitment:** Asked by Abbott for a Texas flag emoji on X, Musk said, "Sure, I will ask the team to make a Texas flag emoji," speaking from the Giga Texas factory, which he noted has a large Texas flag and American flag outside.

Notable quotes (verbatim):
- "SpaceX right now delivers about 85% of all the payloads to orbit of Earth."
- "Hopefully we've established a base on the moon... in 10 years hopefully we've enabled thousands, if not tens of thousands, of people to go to the moon."
- "I think we'll have landed our first people on the moon in less than five years. If things go well, we might be able to put the first astronauts on the moon in two to three years."
- "I think it'd be a heck of a honeymoon trip to take a trip to the moon."
- "I think we'll probably be launching our first AI satellites next year, and then we'll be able to do that at large scale in about two years."
- "I think, if things go well, we can probably send the first people to Mars in about five years."
- "Sure, I will ask the team to make a Texas flag emoji."

interviews.person: Lars Moravy (Vice President of Vehicle Engineering, Tesla)
interviews.venue: Brighter with Herbert (host Herbert, with guest Jeff Lutz)
interviews.summary:
Lars Moravy, Tesla's Vice President of Vehicle Engineering, sat down with Herbert and supply chain executive Jeff Lutz for the Brighter with Herbert platform in an in-person recorded interview on June 30, 2026. The conversation ranged across Cybercab production ramping, Optimus manufacturing buildout, Tesla's AI integration inside factories, competitive philosophy, and vertical integration strategy. The single most newsworthy disclosure was Moravy teasing a "major announcement" tied to the Giga Texas campus scheduled for Tuesday, July 7, 2026, which he said is part of Tesla's broader scaling effort for Cybercab — while declining to elaborate further.

## Cybercab Production Ramp

1. **Lines installed and running, majority of units going to training:** Moravy confirmed that Cybercab production lines at Giga Texas are installed and operational. He said the majority of Cybercabs produced so far have gone into the autonomous training fleet — vehicles fitted with steering wheels and pedals, which he noted with some irony carry the Cybertruck emblem. He described the current phase as a "burn-in process" on a dedicated burn-in track built on the edge of the Giga Texas campus across the highway, explicitly framing every unit built as simultaneously a production unit and a test unit.

2. **~150 units in a burst build; automation "ahead of schedule":** When the interviewer cited a figure of approximately 150 Cybercabs observed, Moravy said "We maybe made 150 — I'll stick with that number." He was careful to distinguish between burst-build quantities and continuous production pace. He added that the automation side is "ahead of schedule," noting he was surprised by the speeds already achievable, and that lines are "over 90% automated all in." He said the teams continue to speed up the automation and work through issues as they build more continuously.

3. **"Production hell" scars as a management advantage:** Moravy said the primary cultural difference in the Cybercab ramp versus earlier programs (Model 3, Cybertruck) is "fear" — deep organizational memory of production hell — combined with significantly more virtual commissioning. He described building everything virtually before machines go online, coding within the virtual environment, and not shipping machines without pre-testing, resulting in better first-time performance. He contrasted this with Model T/Model A and noted Tesla's Model Y global four-factory simultaneous changeover "last year" (i.e., 2025) took three to four weeks, which he called perhaps the largest automated production changeover since Ford's 1914 transition.

4. **Scaling ambition and platform status:** Moravy stated Tesla believes it will build more Cybercabs than anything else it has ever built, positioning it as its own platform. He used the analogy of hard disk drives being displaced by solid-state flash memory — everything about the new technology was better (cheaper, faster, more reliable, more durable) with only initial cost as a drawback, and hard disks largely disappeared within ten to fifteen years. He said Cybercab is in a similar position for transportation: cheaper, safer, more reliable, more efficient. He said whether other vehicles need to be built on the Cybercab platform will depend on adoption rates of autonomous vehicles.

5. **Teaser for July 7 announcement:** Moravy voluntarily disclosed — twice in the transcript — that "in a week from Tuesday, there'll be some cool news about things happening on the campus of Texas," referring to July 7, 2026. He linked this directly to the scaling effort for Cybercab and declined to give any further detail.

6. **Efficiency as the underestimated variable:** When asked what people are most underestimating about Cybercab, Moravy said it is efficiency — not in watt-hours per mile, but in the end-to-end cost from raw material in to vehicle out. He said published autonomous vehicle business forecasts from firms like ARK or Wells Fargo do not actually understand the operational cost structure that Tesla will achieve. He attributed this to Tesla's uniquely vertical position: sourcing metal from ingot and pellets, building compute in-house, writing its own software, owning charging infrastructure, and owning service. He also said he believes vehicle efficiency still has roughly 10–15% to cut, naming mass efficiency as a personal passion.

7. **Consumer sales bet reference:** The host raised Elon Musk's publicized bet with MKBHD that a Cybercab would be sold to a consumer by end of 2026. Moravy declined to engage with the specifics of the bet, saying "I don't know what Elon's doing these days in terms of bets," but affirmed: "we made a product, it's safe, it's functionally safe, it's built on there and the deployment will happen."

## Optimus Production Buildout (Fremont)

1. **First line landed and install underway:** Moravy confirmed that the first Optimus production line has "landed" at the Fremont factory, with installation already underway. He said the automation groups building the equipment are based in the Midwest and in Germany, and those machines are going through the final stages of FAT (Field Acceptance Testing) — getting parts to the automation groups to test machines before shipping to Fremont.

2. **Modular line design enabling rapid commissioning:** Because Tesla knew the Optimus line would require frequent changes, it was designed to be modular. Moravy said the smaller physical scale of Optimus (relative to a car) means commissioning can be very fast: theoretically, a line can be taken down, shipped, reassembled, powered on, and back running within two to three days, with full operation restored within about a week. He said this is "proving out" on the first line.

3. **"40 more to go":** Moravy said there are approximately 40 more Optimus production lines to install after the first. He contextualized this by noting the large number of subsystems — actuators, limbs, torso, battery — each requiring dedicated lines. He described the layout as tributary/unboxed in philosophy, feeding into a small final assembly, similar to Cybercab's architecture but adapted for a 3D multi-axis product.

4. **Manufacturing expertise fully transfers:** Moravy was emphatic that Tesla's automotive manufacturing expertise — supply chain management, multi-sourcing, vendor management, material flow, force majeure robustness — transfers entirely to Optimus. He noted the people designing the Optimus lines are the same individuals who designed Tesla's car lines, and the automation groups building the equipment are the same groups. He also stated that the bill-of-materials cost of a car is higher than a robot, meaning car manufacturing actually demands higher precision and uptime standards than Optimus, making Tesla's experience directly and favorably applicable.

5. **Three competitive advantages for Optimus:** Moravy reiterated (attributing the framing to Elon Musk) that Tesla has three things other humanoid robot companies lack: (1) scale manufacturing capability, (2) proprietary high-power-dense actuators and electric motors that no one else has at volume, and (3) real-world AI implementation. He said: "You only need three for a chair, so it's probably good enough."

6. **Humanoid form factor first, then expansion:** Moravy said Tesla's current focus for Optimus is on "limbic resonance" — making the robot feel like it belongs in human spaces so people become comfortable with it. He said once society accepts robots in workplaces and homes, expansion into other form factors (what he called the "R2-D2 world") will follow naturally. He said it is important to start with the C3PO humanoid form factor.

## AI Integration Inside Tesla's Operations

1. **Four key factory and engineering AI use cases:** Moravy outlined four main internal AI applications: (a) a proprietary internal agent aggregating decades of engineering lessons learned — failure data, test results, design history — so any engineer can search it instantly rather than hunting through people or physical archives; (b) anomaly detection and trending on manufacturing KPIs, particularly catching confluence-of-events failures that spec limits alone would not flag, led by a quality data team he called out specifically; (c) AI-linked manufacturing operating systems that now "think to each other" — for example, body-fit scan data from end-of-line immediately triggering upstream process changes, which Moravy connected to Tesla reaching number three in J.D. Power IQS (announced approximately two days before the interview); (d) service knowledge propagation — a fix discovered by one service technician in one city is now surfaced automatically to technicians everywhere, reducing service times.

2. **"Full Self-Hearing" as a concrete example:** Moravy shared that Tesla cars now drive themselves autonomously from the end of the production line to the logistics yard, and also drive themselves over the bump, squeak, and rattle test track, using cabin microphones to listen for noises and document findings for production teams. He called this internally "full self-hearing." He noted it requires training to map frequencies from locations to specific root causes (e.g., loose door panel clips), with human review still in the loop for edge cases.

3. **Software teams and code generation:** Moravy said Tesla's software teams have been "massively benefited" by AI code generation for some time, using it to produce base code before engineers tackle the hard differentiated work. He also mentioned a company-wide morning digest tool that prepares all 140,000 employees with their schedules and relevant pre-reading.

4. **Internal trials of Macrohard:** When asked whether Tesla is "eating its own dog food" with tools like Macrohard, Moravy said "we are trialing certain things within the company" and left it at that, declining to elaborate.

## Competitive Philosophy and Manufacturing Culture

1. **Waymo efficiency comparison:** Moravy said Waymo's approach — buying a car and adding compute on top — is "probably not efficient enough." He acknowledged that Zoox "gets it" because they also started from a clean sheet. He positioned Cybercab as the correct approach for long-term cost-per-mile competitiveness.

2. **Flat engineering leadership as execution engine:** Moravy emphasized that Tesla's speed and willingness to take calculated risks derives from engineers leading engineers, without layers of program managers or product managers. He gave the example of a vehicle dynamics engineer emailing him and the head of firmware with FSD UX ideas and receiving substantive replies within twenty minutes. He described this as "servant leadership" that is often misunderstood about Tesla.

3. **Rolling changes and risk framing:** On Tesla's practice of rolling changes into live Model 3 and Y production lines, Moravy reframed "risk" as probability of success or failure — arguing that when you understand the impact and can assess probability of improvement, better judgments follow. He said Tesla's leaders understand the engineering deeply enough to make those calls without MBA-style risk frameworks.

4. **Vertical integration and tariff resilience:** Moravy said Tesla's vertical integration — including designing its own PCBs — was decisive during COVID chip shortages (enabling real-time component substitutions over phone calls with suppliers). He noted Tesla placed number one and two on the American-Made Index, which he attributed to understanding supply chains down to tier-three and tier-four levels. He mentioned Tesla shuffled which factory served Canada three times in 2026 in response to tariff changes, calling localization an effective buffer.

5. **SpaceX collaboration:** Moravy said he communicates regularly with SpaceX counterparts (naming Bill, Mike, and John without surnames) and described the two companies as "one mindset." He confirmed Starlink is being explored as a connectivity option for Cybercab, particularly for rural areas. He mentioned SpaceX uses Tesla drive units on Starship, and referenced Terafab as a joint project that is "back together again." He also briefly mentioned the Roadster and ongoing manufacturing integration discussions.

## Five-Year Outlook

1. **Real-world AI everywhere:** When asked what people would be most surprised Tesla accomplished in five years, Moravy said: "The amount of real-world AI that's going to be around you because of us is going to be mind-blowing." He specified this means robotaxis, Cybercabs, Optimus in workplaces and homes, and "everything else we have planned that we aren't even talking about."

Notable quotes (verbatim):
- "We built Cybercab for scale right... we believe that Cybercab does that and it's built for scale."
- "The automation is ahead of schedule actually. I'm sort of impressed that the rates we're able to achieve already, the speed anyway."
- "Lines over over 90% automated all in."
- "I think the amount of real world AI that's going to be around you because of us is going to be mind-blowing."
- "We maybe made 150 — I'll stick with that number if that's what you think we built."
- "In a week from Tuesday, there'll be some cool news about things happening on the campus of Texas and I can't talk about it right now, but that's part of the scaling effort."
- "We call it full self-hearing."
- "We have three things that a lot of other humanoid robot manufacturers don't... we have the scale manufacturing... we have the design of actuators and high volume high power dense electric motors that no one else has... and then we have the real world AI implementation. You only need three for a chair, so it's probably good enough."
- "Elon's been pushing us since 2014, right? So we've been planning a lot of moves over the years to get us to a place where we're ready to do this at a level that I don't think anyone else really really can."
- "Fear... scars like deep wounded like unhealable scars... that's actually very effective."
- "We made a product. It's safe. It's functionally safe. It's built on there and the deployment will happen."
- "The bomb cost of a car is more than a robot. So it's actually more critical to have those things be repeatable and reliable and have high uptime on a higher bomb cost product."
- "I think that the most important thing that Elon has been pushing with the first iteration of Optimus with the team is limbic resonance. It's got to feel like it belongs in our space."

interviews.venue: SpaceX internal/public technical update, Bastrop TX (Terafab/Starlink production facility)
interviews.format: other — informal on-site briefing/walkthrough with SpaceX team
interviews.summary:
Elon Musk joined Ian Doll of SpaceX's Starlink team for an on-site technical briefing at SpaceX's Bastrop, Texas facility — the same building where Starlink user terminals are manufactured and where AI satellite production is being stood up. The conversation ranged from civilizational energy philosophy to concrete engineering plans for orbital AI compute infrastructure, covering Starship reusability milestones, the debut of the "AI1" satellite design, and a Terafab chip-manufacturing megaproject. The single most newsworthy disclosure was SpaceX's stated ambition to reach an annualized rate of 1 gigawatt of space-based AI compute by end of 2027, scaling by an order of magnitude per year thereafter toward a terawatt — framed not as a promise but as "what we are going to try to do and think we probably can do."

## Kardashev Scale and Civilizational Energy Context

1. **Framing the mission through the Kardashev scale:** Musk opened by explaining why the Kardashev scale — proposed by Russian physicist Kardashev — is "the most objective metric" for measuring civilizational progress. A Type I civilization harnesses its planet's available power; Type II harnesses its star's output; Type III harnesses its galaxy's. Musk stated that humanity currently uses "much less than a trillionth of the power output of the sun," meaning civilization is not even registering on the Kardashev 2 scale. He called reaching one-millionth of solar output ("one microsol") "an epic achievement relative to where we are right now" and described it as SpaceX's aspirational goal.

2. **Why space is the only path forward:** Musk argued that even getting to a millionth of solar power would require increasing civilizational energy capture by "much more than a million" times, which is impossible solely on Earth given that 70% of the planet is ocean, much of the remaining land is polar or otherwise unusable, and terrestrial cooling is harder than radiating waste heat into the vacuum of space. He concluded: "In order to ascend the Kardashev scale… you have to go to space."

## Starship and Mass-to-Orbit

3. **Reusability as the foundational breakthrough:** Musk described Starship as "the first rocket design that is capable of full and rapid reusability," calling reusability "the fundamental breakthrough necessary to make life multiplanetary." He drew an analogy to aviation: discarding a rocket after each flight is as impractical as discarding an airplane. The Mechazilla tower catch system — which avoids the mass penalty of landing legs — was cited as a key enabler.

4. **Full reusability milestone targeted "later this year":** Musk stated SpaceX has not yet achieved full reusability but "expect to achieve that hopefully later this year with Starship" (i.e., by end of 2026). Beyond that, the goal is rapid reusability — landing, catching, returning to the launch stand, and reflying "without any refurbishment or laborious inspection like an aircraft." He added that SpaceX expects Starship to eventually fly "more than once per hour."

5. **Starship V3 and V4 performance figures:** Musk stated Starship B3 (Version 3, flown on Flight 12) produces "more than double the thrust of the Saturn V moon rocket." By Version 4, he expects thrust to reach "pretty much three times" that of Saturn V. Ian Doll noted that Flight 12's payload was the heaviest SpaceX has ever flown, yet still only a fraction of V3's full capability.

6. **Scale of mass-to-orbit ambitions:** Musk stated SpaceX currently delivers "almost 90%" (or "between 85 and 90%") of all Earth mass to orbit, with the remainder mostly launched by China. Current annual mass to orbit stands at roughly 2,500 tons per year. He stated SpaceX aims to reach "a million tons to orbit per year in about 3 years" (i.e., approximately 2029).

## AI1 Satellite Design

7. **The AI1 satellite unveiled:** Ian Doll walked through a draft design for SpaceX's first AI satellite, dubbed "AI1." The reference design targets 150 kW peak power and 120 kW sustained average compute power — roughly matching an Nvidia GB300 rack with 72 GPUs (which peaks at ~140 kW but rarely reaches that in practice). Musk described it as conceptually simpler than a Starlink satellite: "essentially a lot of solar cells, a radiator," and laser links, without the complex phased-array and parabolic antennas of Starlink.

8. **Physical specifications of the AI1:** Solar arrays assume 250 W per square meter; radiators (double-sided, oriented knife-edge to the sun) assume 1,400 W per square meter. Musk noted both figures are "very achievable" and expected to improve over time. The satellite has approximately a 70-meter wingspan. Planned orbital altitude is approximately 600–800 km; at that distance, round-trip latency is roughly 3 milliseconds ("light travels 300 km per millisecond"). Connectivity is planned at approximately 1 terabit of laser-link bandwidth.

9. **Leveraging existing Starlink manufacturing technology:** Doll emphasized that the solar array technology for AI1 is derived from what SpaceX is already developing for Starlink V3 satellites, making the engineering challenge "not a super hard problem compared to things we already do." The radiators are described as roughly the same size as existing V3 solar arrays.

10. **Chip options and current reference design:** Musk stated the current reference design supports Nvidia Rubin chips (or GB300), with an additional reference design for TPUs. He added that "essentially you can put any existing chips into orbit."

## Production and Terafab

11. **Bastrop becoming the AI satellite production hub:** Musk confirmed that a solar manufacturing facility is already under construction at Bastrop. An AI satellite production building ("AIAT production building") will follow. He stated SpaceX expects "AI satellite production, solar production, and all of that operating at some reasonable volume by the end of next year" (i.e., by end of 2027). Doll noted the existing Bastrop facility continues to produce Starlink user terminals, with new production lines being added. Musk stated the total addressable market for Starlink terminals could reach "a few hundred million."

12. **Terafab — a 100-million-square-foot chip megafactory:** To scale beyond what the current global chip industry can deliver (~100 GW/year of AI compute), Musk described the Terafab — a proposed chip fabrication facility roughly 100 million square feet in size, "10 times the size of the Tesla Gigafactory Texas." He described it as fundamentally about scale rather than novel technology breakthroughs, with a target output of 1 terawatt of chips per year — equivalent to "a billion full-reticle-equivalent chips each doing a kilowatt."

## Orbital AI Compute Scaling Roadmap

13. **Stated scaling trajectory (explicitly framed as a target, not a promise):** Musk offered the following trajectory for space-based AI compute: reaching an annualized rate of 1 GW/year by end of 2027 (end of next year); 10 GW/year by approximately mid-2028 (~2.5 years out); 100 GW/year by approximately mid-2029 (~3.5 years out); and eventually scaling to 1 TW/year (1,000 GW), which Musk noted is "twice the current electricity consumption of the United States." He explicitly prefaced this: "people should take this with a grain of salt… this is not a promise of what we'll do. This is what we are going to try to do and think we probably can do."

## Moon-Based Infrastructure as Next Frontier

14. **Lunar mass driver for post-terawatt scaling:** Musk described the path beyond 1 TW/year as requiring lunar infrastructure. Because the moon has no atmosphere and only 1/6 Earth's gravity, AI satellites could be launched from the moon's surface using an electromagnetic mass driver (a "rail gun" or "linear electric motor") rather than rockets. Local production of photovoltaics, solar panels, and radiators on the moon would avoid the need to transport mass from Earth. Musk said chips could be brought from Earth or "conceivably" manufactured on the moon. He framed this as the path to "another three orders of magnitude" — 1,000x beyond a terawatt.

15. **Moon access as a byproduct:** Musk added that if sufficient mass is being delivered to the moon to support this infrastructure, "anyone who wants to go to the moon will be able to go to the moon," and expressed that "everyone should go to the moon at least once."

## Notable Quotes (verbatim):

- "We're not even registering. Not even a microsoul. Yeah. One microsoul would be an epic, epic achievement relative to where we are right now."
- "We we haven't achieved full reusability yet, but we do expect to achieve that hopefully later this year with Starship."
- "We expect Starship to be flying more than once per hour down the road."
- "We think probably we can get to a million tons to orbit per year in about 3 years thereabouts."
- "This is not a promise of what we'll do. This is what we are going to try to do and think we probably can do — which is to get to roughly an annualized rate of a gigawatt per year by the end of next year in terms of space AI compute."
- "Aspirationally scale that by an order of magnitude per year. So in 2 and a half years hitting an annualized rate of 10 gigawatt a year to space, in 3 and a half years maybe 100 gigawatt."
- "The terafab is going to be around 100 million square feet, which is 10 times the size of the Tesla Gigafactory Texas."

claims.claim: SpaceX expects to achieve full Starship reusability later in 2026

claims.claim: Starship will eventually fly more than once per hour

claims.claim: Starship V4 will produce roughly three times the thrust of the Saturn V moon rocket

claims.claim: SpaceX targets an annualized rate of 1 GW/year of space-based AI compute by end of 2027
claims.timeframe: by the end of next year (end of 2027)

claims.claim: SpaceX targets 10 GW/year of space-based AI compute approximately 2.5 years from now (~late 2028)
claims.quote: Aspirationally scale that by an order of magnitude per year. So in 2 and a half years hitting an annualized rate of 10 gigawatt a year to space.

claims.claim: SpaceX targets 100 GW/year of space-based AI compute approximately 3.5 years from now (~late 2029)

claims.claim: SpaceX aspires to eventually scale space-based AI compute to 1 terawatt per year (1,000 GW)

claims.claim: Terafab is targeted to output 1 terawatt of chips per year

claims.claim: Lunar mass driver infrastructure is the pathway to scaling space-based AI compute by another 1,000x beyond a terawatt
claims.quote: In order to get to another three orders of magnitude to 1000x from a terowatt per year, the only way that we can really see that you can achieve that is on the moon with a mass driver essentially where you do local production of photovoltaics and solar and radiators on the moon.
